```{r gallery-setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4.8, dpi = 144, out.width = "100%")
library(postrank)
source(system.file("scripts", "_vignette-setup.R", package = "postrank", mustWork = TRUE), local = TRUE)
one <- load_or_compute("tutorial_one")
two <- load_or_compute("tutorial_two")
frontier <- load_or_compute("tutorial_frontier")
commonality <- load_or_compute("tutorial_commonality")
comparison <- load_or_compute("comparison_30x3_tau35")
```

Seven graphical summaries describe the posterior information, grading
decision and associated losses. Each plotting function returns a `ggplot`
object based on prepared information, without further optimization,
posterior estimation or calculation of comparison probabilities.
The initial examples use the specified normal distributions for six sites in
[Getting started](a1-getting-started.html); a separate comparison below uses
the additional 30-site synthetic example.

The distribution of score A is unchanged when score B is included. Both scores
have standard deviation 0.2, sites and criteria are independent, and higher
values have higher priority. Grade 1 is highest. These sites have no empirical
interpretation. A shared grade withholds a comparison; it does not assert
that the true scores coincide.

## 1. Marginal posterior intervals and grades {#where-are-the-uncertain-scores-and-chosen-grades}

The report card displays marginal posterior intervals alongside the
selected grades. For one criterion, sites are represented on a common score
axis. The intervals describe uncertainty about the targets; they do not
represent probabilities of grade membership.

```{r gallery-card, fig.alt="Score-A marginal intervals for sites A through F, colored by the three chosen grades."}
postrank_plot_report_card(one)
```

For several criteria, separate panels accommodate differences in units.
Display labels are separate from the stable entity identifiers. The default row limit is 30;
selection is spread across grades and disclosed in the subtitle. Explicit
`entities` can select a larger report. Ordering by the posterior mean requires a single displayed criterion or
an explicit `order_by` naming the criterion that defines the order.

## 2. Disclosed and withheld comparisons {#which-comparisons-did-the-report-disclose}

The relations plot represents the grading decision, with colour indicating
the disclosed direction or withholding of each comparison. The cells encode
actions rather than posterior probabilities. In particular, a withheld
comparison does not imply a posterior probability of one half.

```{r gallery-relations, fig.alt="Pair relations in the common two-score grade: A through D share a grade, followed by E and F."}
postrank_plot_relations(two)
```

Only order and equality of grade labels matter. Replacing occupied labels
by other increasing integers preserves every relation. The same plot is
available for a prepared fit or baseline, including an all-withheld
action. When no validated incumbent is available, the display reports the
computational status.

## 3. Criterion-specific errors and losses {#how-does-each-criterion-contribute}

Criterion profiles report posterior expected errors per disclosed pair,
expected errors per all pairs, or posterior loss. The default is expected
errors per disclosed pair; `show = "E_over_M"` and `show = "risk"` select
the other quantities. Equal loss weights need not produce equal
criterion-specific errors under the common grading.

```{r gallery-profile, fig.alt="Expected wrong-direction errors per disclosed pair by criterion for the common two-score action."}
postrank_plot_profile(two)
```

`E/N` is undefined when nothing is disclosed and remains unavailable;
`E/M` can then be zero. These quantities are ratios of posterior expected counts and do not
estimate classification accuracy in an external sample. Budget lines appear only
when corresponding budgets were declared. Zero-weight criteria remain
visible with their weight identified.

## 4. Directional-error probabilities {#what-probabilities-were-supplied-to-the-decision}

The pairwise plot describes the input to the grading problem. Each cell
contains the stored probability of an incorrect declaration placing the
row entity above the column entity. These probabilities are calculated
before optimization.

```{r gallery-pairwise, fig.alt="Directional-error probability matrices for score A and score B; gray diagonal cells are unavailable self-comparisons."}
postrank_plot_pairwise(two, ncol = 2L)
```

Ordinary tie-free coefficients use the event
\(P(\theta_{i,k}\leq\theta_{j,k}\mid Y)\). Self-comparisons, shown in grey, are `NA` rather
than zero-error comparisons. By default, the display selects at most 20
entities and reports the selection; all six sites are included here. The
function accepts prepared ordinary coefficients, including supported
probability inputs. Raw draws and the separate equality-neutral domain
are outside its input scope.

## 5. Comparison of grading rules {#how-do-grading-rules-compare-under-the-same-loss}

This example uses 30 synthetic sites on three criteria, with
`weights = c(poverty = .5, frl = .25, snap = .25)`, `tau = .35` and at most
four grades. The names are illustrative and do not identify observed poverty or
school eligibility measures. The joint and fixed-order baseline actions are evaluated
under this one posterior and loss.

```{r gallery-comparison, fig.height=7, fig.alt="Risk, disclosure and grade-count panels comparing the prepared joint report with fixed-order baselines on the same 30-site posterior and loss."}
postrank_plot_compare(comparison, ncol = 1L)
```

The method labels include computational status, optimization scope and gap. A fixed-order optimum applies to
contiguous cuts of that score order, rather than every grading. A supplied
action outside the reference constraints is marked accordingly; its risk
can still be scored but is not a minimum over the same feasible family.
The relations view, `view = "relations"`, counts newly disclosed, newly
withheld and reversed comparisons against the reference.

## 6. Sensitivity to the withholding cost {#what-changes-when-withholding-costs-more}

For the six-site example with equal weights on the two scores, the
prepared frontier varies tau through .05, .1, .2, .3 and .4. The inputs
and the family of gradings with at most three grades are held fixed.

```{r gallery-frontier, fig.alt="Disclosure and error summaries at five withholding costs for the six-site common grade."}
postrank_plot_frontier(frontier)
```

For exact optima in a fixed family, disclosure is nondecreasing in tau.
For numerical solutions, interpretation also depends on the stored
optimization gaps. A sparse grid describes only part of the frontier. Missing actions appear as breaks in the plotted path. Risks at different tau values use different
losses. Preparing a new frontier calls an optimizer; displaying this stored
one does not.

## 7. Criterion-specific costs of a common grading {#what-does-each-criterion-give-up-for-a-common-grade}

The commonality view compares each criterion's risk under the common report
with its own best risk under the same tau and grade-count settings. Preparing
this object solves an own-criterion problem for each criterion.

```{r gallery-commonality, fig.alt="Criterion-specific commonality costs with intervals determined by numerical optimization bounds."}
postrank_plot_commonality(commonality)
```

The interval is determined by numerical bounds for the own-criterion
problem and does not quantify posterior uncertainty about the cost.
Incomplete optimization may therefore yield a range of possible costs. When the common problem includes protection constraints, the own-criterion
comparison family depends on whether these constraints are retained.
Their treatment must therefore be reported with the result. The tutorial has no such
budgets.

## Underlying tables and figure export {#inspect-and-export}

The full underlying table is available through
`postrank_plot_data(two, "profile")` or another supported component. Display row limits and labels do not change those
tables. `ggplot2::ggsave()` exports the returned plots; optional `svglite`
provides SVG output. See [Figures and sensitivity analysis](a7-figures-sensitivity.html)
for dimensions and explicit recomputation examples, and
[Reading and exporting results](a6-reading-exporting-results.html) for tables
and reports. No public plotting functions are provided for the additional reserved
figures in this candidate.
